description: Shabbat, the High Holy Days and the Pilgrim Festivals: Pesach, Sukkot and Shavuot.
content_html:
Shabbat: The Day of Rest

Shabbat is the most important weekly observance in Judaism. Its authority rests in Genesis 2:1–3, where G‑d rested on the seventh day after creation, and in Exodus 20:8–11, which commands: “Remember the Sabbath day by keeping it holy.” For observant Jews, Shabbat is not merely a day off but a foretaste of the Messianic Age — a sign of the covenant between G‑d and Israel.

Shabbat begins at sunset on Friday and ends on Saturday night, when three stars are visible. Preparation is essential: the home is cleaned, special meals are cooked in advance, and family members are dressed in their best clothes. At the Friday night table, the woman of the household lights two candles while reciting a blessing, welcoming the peace of Shabbat. Wine is sanctified in the Kiddush prayer, and two plaited loaves (challah) are blessed to recall the double portion of manna given in the wilderness.

Key Fact

Traditional Jewish law identifies 39 categories of work (melachah) prohibited on Shabbat, derived from the types of labour used to build the Tabernacle. These include lighting fire, writing, cooking, carrying objects in a public place, and — in modern Orthodox interpretation — using electricity. Orthodox Jews do not drive, use phones or watch television on Shabbat.

At the end of Shabbat, the Havdalah ceremony separates the holy day from the rest of the week. A braided candle is lit, spices are smelled (a symbol of the sweetness of Shabbat being carried into the week), wine is blessed and drunk, then the candle is extinguished by dipping it into the few remaining drops. Reform Jews may observe Shabbat more liberally — driving to synagogue, for example — seeing the spirit of rest rather than specific restrictions as primary.

Orthodox Jews follow all 39 categories of melachah strictly, believing they are part of the binding Oral Law. Eruv areas (symbolic boundaries in cities) allow carrying within them on Shabbat. Reform Jews hold that the Torah’s principles must be applied with reason to modern life: they may use electricity or travel by car to attend synagogue, seeing the communal and spiritual aspects as more important than the technical prohibitions. Both communities celebrate Kiddush, candle lighting and the Shabbat meal as the heart of the day.

Rosh Hashanah: Jewish New Year

Rosh Hashanah opens the High Holy Days in autumn. It is a solemn celebration: the birthday of creation and the day on which G‑d is said to judge all people. The shofar (ram’s horn) is blown up to 100 times during synagogue services, recalling the ram caught in the thicket in place of Isaac and calling worshippers to self-examination. Symbolic foods eaten at the meal include apples dipped in honey — expressing hope for a sweet new year — and pomegranates, whose seeds represent the wish to fulfil as many good deeds as its seeds.

The most distinctive ritual is Tashlich, where Jews walk to a river or stream and throw breadcrumbs into the water to symbolise casting away their sins. Central to the spirit of Rosh Hashanah is Teshuva — turning away from wrongdoing and returning to G‑d — which takes place over the ten days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur.

Yom Kippur: The Day of Atonement

Yom Kippur falls ten days after Rosh Hashanah. It is the holiest day in the Jewish calendar. Five prohibitions apply for the full 25-hour fast: eating and drinking, washing for pleasure, wearing leather shoes, applying cosmetics, and marital relations. These privations reflect total focus on spiritual purification rather than physical comfort.

Synagogue services on Yom Kippur are the longest of the year. The day opens with Kol Nidre, a moving declaration that annuls vows made to G‑d. During the day, worshippers recite the Vidui (confession) repeatedly, beating their chest at each sin. The Book of Life — a metaphor for G‑d’s record of human deeds — is said to be sealed on Yom Kippur; the greeting exchanged is “G‑mar chatimah tovah” (“may you be inscribed for good”). The fast ends with Neilah, the closing service, followed by a single blast of the shofar. The concept of Kapparah (atonement) is at the heart of the day.

Key Fact

Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur together form the High Holy Days (Yamim Noraim — “Days of Awe”). Rosh Hashanah opens the Book of Life; Yom Kippur seals it. The shofar is blown at Rosh Hashanah and once more at the end of Yom Kippur to mark closure.

The Pilgrim Festivals

Three festivals are called the Pilgrim Festivals: Pesach, Shavuot and Sukkot. In biblical times, all Jewish men were commanded to appear at the Temple in Jerusalem for each of these three festivals (Exodus 12:14–15 addresses Pesach).

Pesach (Passover) commemorates the Exodus from Egypt, when G‑d freed the Israelites from slavery under Pharaoh. All leavened bread (chametz) is removed from the home before the festival. The central event is the Seder meal, during which the Haggadah (a special text) is read, recounting the Exodus narrative. Symbolic foods — matzah (unleavened bread), bitter herbs, salt water, a lamb shank bone and charoset (a sweet paste) — each represent part of the Exodus story. The meal reinforces the idea that every Jew in every generation should see themselves as if they personally came out of Egypt.

Sukkot follows Yom Kippur and lasts seven days. Families build a temporary shelter called a sukkah with a roof of natural materials through which the stars can be seen, recalling the booths in which the Israelites lived in the desert (Leviticus 23:42–43). The four species (arba minim) — a palm branch (lulav), myrtle, willow and citron (etrog) — are waved together in all directions as a symbol of G‑d’s presence everywhere.

Shavuot falls 50 days after Pesach and celebrates G‑d giving the Torah to Moses at Sinai, as well as the early summer harvest. Synagogues and homes are decorated with flowers and greenery. Many Jews stay up all night studying Torah (Tikkun Leil Shavuot) to re-enact the receiving of the Law. Dairy foods are traditionally eaten, though the reasons are debated.

Hanukkah is not one of the Pilgrim Festivals but is widely celebrated. It recalls the rededication of the Temple in Jerusalem in 165 BCE after the Maccabees defeated the Seleucid Greeks. Only a small amount of ritually pure oil was found — enough for one day — yet the Temple menorah burned for eight days. A nine-branched hanukkiah is lit, one candle per night (plus the servant candle), in windows so passersby can see the miracle publicised. Special songs are sung and potato latkes (levivot) or doughnuts fried in oil are eaten. Hanukkah has no specific biblical commandment and does not have the same religious status as the Pilgrim Festivals or Yom Kippur.
exam_tip_html: A very common error on Shabbat questions is confusing Kiddush (the blessing over wine) with Havdalah (the ceremony that ends Shabbat). Make sure you can describe each separately. For ‘Explain’ questions about festivals, always state what is done, why it is done (the origin or biblical command), and the significance for believers — this is the Explain depth-pattern. On the 15-mark Discuss, a popular topic is whether Yom Kippur or Pesach is more important: use named sources (Exodus 20:8–11 for Shabbat, Leviticus 23:42–43 for Sukkot, Exodus 12:14–15 for Pesach) to anchor your arguments. Correct spelling of “Teshuva,” “Havdalah” and “Kapparah” is rewarded on the extended response.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Shabbat is the holiest weekly day, beginning with candle lighting and Kiddush on Friday evening and ending with Havdalah; 39 categories of prohibited work apply in Orthodox practice, though Reform Jews observe the spirit of rest more flexibly.
  • Rosh Hashanah (New Year, shofar, Tashlich) and Yom Kippur (fasting, Kol Nidre, Neilah) form the High Holy Days; both focus on Teshuva (repentance) and Kapparah (atonement), with the metaphor of G-d sealing the Book of Life on Yom Kippur.
  • The three Pilgrim Festivals are Pesach (Exodus, Seder meal, chametz removal), Sukkot (sukkah, four species) and Shavuot (receiving the Torah); Hanukkah celebrates the Temple rededication over eight nights but carries less religious weight than the biblical festivals.

practice_questions.text: State what Havdalah marks in Jewish practice.
practice_questions.marks: The end of Shabbat / the separation of Shabbat from the rest of the week. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens during the Seder meal at Pesach.
practice_questions.marks: The Haggadah is read to retell the story of the Exodus from Egypt [1] and symbolic foods including matzah, bitter herbs and salt water are eaten to recall the experience of slavery and liberation [1]. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline the significance of Yom Kippur for Jewish people.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any three of: Yom Kippur is the holiest day in the Jewish calendar; it involves a 25-hour fast during which five physical pleasures are forbidden; worshippers recite the Vidui (confession) and seek Kapparah (atonement); the Neilah service closes the day with a blast of the shofar; Jews believe the Book of Life is sealed on this day. [3 marks — 1 mark each]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which Shabbat is observed differently by Orthodox and Reform Jews.
Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Orthodox Jews follow all 39 prohibited categories of work strictly (e.g. no electricity, no driving), believing these derive from the binding Oral Law and reflect the command in Exodus 20:8-11 to 'keep it holy'. Reform Jews may drive to synagogue, seeing communal worship as more important than technical restrictions.
• In Orthodox communities, the mechitzah (partition) separates men and women at synagogue Shabbat services. Reform synagogues allow mixed seating and women to lead services.
• Both communities share Kiddush, candle lighting and the Shabbat meal, but Orthodox Jews require a minyan of ten men for services; Reform congregations may count women.
[6 marks — 3 marks per difference: 1 for a simple statement, 2 for development, 3 for a relevant source]

practice_questions.text: 'Yom Kippur is the most important Jewish festival.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Yom Kippur is universally regarded as the holiest day (Yom HaKippurim — the Day of Atonements); the full 25-hour fast and five prohibitions show its supreme solemnity.
• The concept of Kapparah and the sealing of the Book of Life make it unique: no other festival carries this weight of judgement and forgiveness.
• Synagogue attendance on Yom Kippur is highest of any day, including among Jews who rarely attend otherwise, showing its central place in Jewish identity.
• Teshuva enables Jews to repair relationships with G-d and with each other in a way no other festival provides.

Arguments against:
• Shabbat is described in Genesis 2:1-3 and the Ten Commandments as the holiest recurring time; Yom Kippur is annual, Shabbat weekly — many rabbis argue Shabbat outweighs all other festivals in obligation.
• Pesach celebrates the defining event of Jewish history — the Exodus from Egypt — and the Seder meal has been practised continuously for millennia. Exodus 12:14-15 calls it 'a lasting ordinance'.
• Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur are closely linked; it is arguably the pair that matters, not Yom Kippur alone.
• Sukkot and Shavuot have equal biblical status as Pilgrim Festivals, all commanded in Torah.

Mastering: Both sides fully developed with named sources (Genesis 2:1-3, Exodus 20:8-11, Exodus 12:14-15, Leviticus 23), different festival traditions compared, and a justified conclusion explaining which festival is most fundamental to Jewish identity.
Secure: Clear arguments on both sides with relevant named sources and a reasoned conclusion.
Developing: Some relevant points with limited source reference; conclusion present but not fully argued.
Emerging: One-sided or brief; little or no source material used. [15 marks — SPaG assessed]

practice_questions.text: Outline three rituals associated with Rosh Hashanah.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any three of: blowing the shofar up to 100 times during the synagogue service; Tashlich — casting breadcrumbs into flowing water to symbolise casting away sins; eating apples dipped in honey to symbolise hope for a sweet new year; eating pomegranates representing the wish to fulfil many commandments; Teshuva — reflecting on wrongdoing and resolving to repent over the ten days to Yom Kippur. [3 marks — 1 mark each]

knowledge_checks.q: What does the Havdalah ceremony mark?
options: The beginning of Shabbat on Friday evening
The separation of Shabbat from the rest of the week at Saturday nightfall
The giving of the Torah at Sinai

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following best describes Tashlich?
options: A closing prayer service at the end of Yom Kippur
The blessing over wine recited on Shabbat
A ceremony of casting breadcrumbs into water to symbolise casting away sins
The four species waved during Sukkot

knowledge_checks.q: During Pesach, all _____ (leavened food) is removed from the home before the festival.
The _____ is the closing prayer service of Yom Kippur, at which the Book of Life is symbolically sealed.
Match each festival to its central ritual or theme:
right: Building a sukkah and waving the four species
Lighting the hanukkiah for eight nights

flashcard_questions.q: What is Shabbat and when does it begin?
flashcard_questions.a: The Jewish day of rest; begins at Friday sunset and ends Saturday nightfall.
The blessing over wine recited to sanctify Shabbat or a festival.
The ritual ceremony that marks the end of Shabbat and separates it from the rest of the week.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the purpose of Tashlich on Rosh Hashanah?
flashcard_questions.a: Symbolically casting sins away by throwing breadcrumbs into flowing water.
Repentance and return to G-d, central to the High Holy Days.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the five prohibitions that apply on Yom Kippur.
flashcard_questions.a: No eating or drinking, washing for pleasure, leather shoes, cosmetics, or marital relations.
Atonement — the spiritual goal of Yom Kippur.
The closing prayer service at the end of Yom Kippur, when the Book of Life is sealed.

flashcard_questions.q: What is chametz and why is it removed at Pesach?
flashcard_questions.a: Leavened food; removed to recall the Israelites' hasty departure from Egypt.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the collective name for the four plant species waved together during Sukkot?

flashcard_questions.a: The rededication of the Temple in 165 BCE and the miracle of oil burning for eight days.

flashcard_questions.q: Which biblical text commands the building of a sukkah?

glossary_terms.definition: The Jewish day of rest observed from Friday sunset to Saturday nightfall, commanded in Genesis 2:1-3 and Exodus 20:8-11.
The blessing over wine recited on Shabbat and festivals to sanctify the day.
The ceremony marking the end of Shabbat, involving blessings over wine, spices and a multi-wicked candle to distinguish Shabbat from the rest of the week.
The Jewish New Year, a two-day festival of reflection and repentance marking the start of the High Holy Days.
Repentance and return to G-d, a key theme of the High Holy Days.
A ceremony performed on Rosh Hashanah in which Jews symbolically cast sins into flowing water, often by emptying their pockets near a river or stream.
The Day of Atonement, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar, observed with fasting and intensive prayer for forgiveness.
Atonement achieved through repentance, prayer and charity on Yom Kippur, sometimes understood as a symbolic transference of sins.
The closing prayer service at the end of Yom Kippur, as the synagogue gates are symbolically shut and the Book of Life is sealed.
Three biblical festivals (Pesach, Shavuot, Sukkot) when Jews in ancient times made pilgrimage to the Temple in Jerusalem.
Passover, the spring festival commemorating the Exodus from Egypt; observed for seven or eight days with the Seder meal and removal of chametz.
Leavened food made with fermenting agents, forbidden in Jewish homes during Pesach in memory of the Israelites' hasty departure from Egypt when there was no time for bread to rise.
The ritual Passover meal at which the story of the Exodus is retold using the Haggadah and symbolic foods including matzah, bitter herbs and salt water.
The autumn harvest festival recalling the Israelites' 40 years in the wilderness; celebrated by building and eating in a temporary shelter (sukkah).
The festival of Weeks, celebrated 50 days after Pesach, marking G-d's gift of the Torah at Sinai and the early harvest.
The Festival of Lights, an eight-day festival recalling the rededication of the Temple in Jerusalem in 165 BCE and the miracle of the oil.
